course.title: Principles of Accounting
course.description: A first course in financial accounting — from the accounting equation and journal entries to the four financial statements and the ratios that read them. Structure adapted from OpenStax Principles of Accounting, Volume 1 (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: The accounting equation states that Assets equal…
questions.explanation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity — the balance that holds in every entry.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the four core financial statements?
questions.explanation: The trial balance is an internal check, not a published statement.

questions.prompt: Increasing an asset account is recorded with a…
questions.explanation: Assets increase on the debit (left) side.

questions.prompt: In every journal entry, total debits must equal…
The step of the accounting cycle that updates accounts for items like used-up supplies is…
questions.explanation: Adjusting entries record amounts earned or used but not yet recorded.

questions.prompt: Revenue is recognized when it is…
questions.explanation: Under accrual accounting, revenue is earned, not necessarily when cash arrives.

questions.prompt: Net income equals…
questions.explanation: Net income = Revenue − Expenses, reported on the income statement.

questions.prompt: The current ratio measures…
questions.explanation: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities, a liquidity measure.

lessons.title: The accounting equation
lessons.grammar_note: Assets = Liabilities + Equity — it must stay balanced after every transaction.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State the accounting equation and show how any transaction keeps it balanced. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what two things sit on the right side of the equation?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Every business is a pile of resources (assets) and the claims on them. Creditors' claims are liabilities; the owner's claim is equity. So Assets = Liabilities + Equity, always. A worked example: Rivera Consulting starts when the owner invests $10,000 cash. Cash (an asset) rises by $10,000 and Capital (equity) rises by $10,000, so $10,000 = $0 + $10,000. The equation holds because both sides moved together.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Continue with Rivera. (a) The firm borrows $5,000 from a bank: Cash +$5,000, Notes Payable +$5,000 → Assets $15,000 = Liabilities $5,000 + Equity $10,000. (b) It buys equipment for $4,000 cash: Equipment +$4,000, Cash −$4,000 → total assets still $15,000, so $15,000 = $5,000 + $10,000. (c) It buys $600 of supplies on account: Supplies +$600, Accounts Payable +$600 → Assets $15,600 = Liabilities $5,600 + Equity $10,000. Each line balances.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: State each transaction's effect and confirm the equation still balances (starting from Assets $15,600 = Liabilities $5,600 + Equity $10,000): (1) collect $2,000 cash for services performed; (2) pay $800 cash for rent; (3) owner withdraws $200 cash; (4) pay $600 owed to the supplier. Answers: (1) Cash +2,000, Equity (revenue) +2,000 → 17,600 = 5,600 + 12,000; (2) Cash −800, Equity (expense) −800 → 16,800 = 5,600 + 11,200; (3) Cash −200, Equity −200 → 16,600 = 5,600 + 11,000; (4) Cash −600, Accounts Payable −600 → 16,000 = 5,000 + 11,000.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting revenue and expenses live inside equity, so they tilt the right side too. Mistake: recording only one side of a transaction. Exit: (a) After all four transactions above, what does Equity equal? (b) Which side of the equation holds liabilities? Answers: $11,000; the right side.

lessons.title: Debits, credits, and journal entries
lessons.grammar_note: Debits = left, credits = right; in every entry the two must be equal.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Apply the debit/credit rules and write balanced journal entries. Warm-up: increasing an asset — debit or credit?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Debit just means the left side of an account and credit the right side; neither means 'good' or 'bad'. The rule follows the equation: assets and expenses increase with debits; liabilities, equity, and revenue increase with credits. Because every transaction touches both sides of Assets = Liabilities + Equity, total debits must equal total credits. Worked example — Rivera's owner invests $10,000: Debit Cash $10,000; Credit Capital $10,000. Debits $10,000 = Credits $10,000.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: More Rivera entries, each self-balancing. (a) Buy equipment for cash: Debit Equipment $4,000; Credit Cash $4,000. (b) Perform services for cash: Debit Cash $2,000; Credit Service Revenue $2,000. (c) Pay rent: Debit Rent Expense $800; Credit Cash $800. (d) Buy supplies on account: Debit Supplies $600; Credit Accounts Payable $600. In every entry the debit total equals the credit total, so the books stay in balance.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Journalize each and check debits = credits: (1) borrow $5,000 on a note; (2) owner withdraws $200 cash; (3) pay $600 owed to a supplier; (4) buy $300 of supplies for cash. Answers: (1) Debit Cash 5,000 / Credit Notes Payable 5,000; (2) Debit Owner's Drawings 200 / Credit Cash 200; (3) Debit Accounts Payable 600 / Credit Cash 600; (4) Debit Supplies 300 / Credit Cash 300. Each entry balances.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a debit always increases an account — it depends on the account type. Mistake: leaving an entry one-sided. Exit: (a) Revenue increases with a debit or a credit? (b) If you debit Rent Expense $800, what do you credit? Answers: a credit; Cash $800.

lessons.title: The four financial statements
lessons.grammar_note: Order matters: income statement → statement of owner's equity → balance sheet → cash flows.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the four financial statements and show how numbers flow from one to the next. Warm-up: which statement reports Revenue minus Expenses?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Four statements tell the story in order. The income statement shows Revenue − Expenses = Net Income. The statement of owner's equity rolls net income into the owner's claim. The balance sheet snapshots Assets = Liabilities + Equity on a date. The statement of cash flows explains the change in cash. Each feeds the next, so they must agree. Worked example — Rivera's month: Revenue $2,000 − Rent Expense $800 = Net Income $1,200.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Build Rivera's statements from the running example. Statement of owner's equity: Investment $10,000 + Net Income $1,200 − Drawings $200 = Ending Capital $11,000. Balance sheet — Assets: Cash $12,000 + Supplies $600 + Equipment $4,000 = $16,600; Liabilities: Notes Payable $5,000 + Accounts Payable $600 = $5,600; Equity: Capital $11,000. Check: $5,600 + $11,000 = $16,600, so Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Cash reconciles too: 10,000 + 5,000 − 4,000 + 2,000 − 800 − 200 = $12,000.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer from Rivera's statements: (1) What is net income? (2) What is ending capital? (3) What are total assets? (4) Does the balance sheet balance, and by what total? Answers: (1) $1,200; (2) $11,000; (3) $16,600; (4) yes — both sides equal $16,600.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: putting the owner's withdrawal on the income statement (it belongs on the equity statement, not among expenses). Mistake: expecting cash to equal net income. Exit: (a) Which statement links net income to equity? (b) Assets = Liabilities + ___? Answers: the statement of owner's equity; Equity.

questions.prompt: After an owner invests $10,000 cash, the equation reads…
Buying $4,000 of equipment for cash changes total assets by…
questions.explanation: One asset rises and another falls by the same amount — no net change.

questions.prompt: To record services performed for cash you would…
questions.explanation: Cash (asset) up with a debit; revenue up with a credit.

questions.prompt: In a balanced entry, if Rent Expense is debited $800, then $800 is credited to…
questions.explanation: Paying rent in cash credits Cash $800, so debits equal credits.

questions.prompt: Which statement reports the balance Assets = Liabilities + Equity on a specific date?
questions.explanation: The balance sheet is the dated snapshot.

lessons.title: The accounting cycle and adjusting entries
lessons.grammar_note: Adjust before you report: match revenues and expenses to the period they belong to.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: List the accounting cycle steps and write adjusting entries that keep the books balanced. Warm-up: which cycle step comes right before preparing the statements?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The accounting cycle runs: analyze → journalize → post → unadjusted trial balance → adjust → adjusted trial balance → prepare statements → close. Adjusting entries fix timing: they record revenue earned or expense incurred that cash hasn't yet captured. Like all entries they balance. Worked example — Rivera bought $600 of supplies and $250 are used up: Debit Supplies Expense $250; Credit Supplies $250. Supplies on the books drop to $350, and debits equal credits.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Three more month-end adjustments for Rivera, each balancing. (a) Prepaid insurance of $1,200 covers 12 months; one month expires: Debit Insurance Expense $100; Credit Prepaid Insurance $100. (b) Equipment depreciates $100 this month: Debit Depreciation Expense $100; Credit Accumulated Depreciation $100. (c) $500 of services were performed but not yet billed: Debit Accounts Receivable $500; Credit Service Revenue $500. In each, the debit equals the credit, so the adjusted trial balance still ties out.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Write the adjusting entry and note the account type: (1) $150 of supplies remain from $600 recorded, so $450 were used; (2) accrued wages of $300 owed but unpaid; (3) $400 of a $1,200 prepaid rent has expired; (4) $250 of unearned fees are now earned. Answers: (1) Debit Supplies Expense 450 / Credit Supplies 450; (2) Debit Wages Expense 300 / Credit Wages Payable 300; (3) Debit Rent Expense 400 / Credit Prepaid Rent 400; (4) Debit Unearned Revenue 250 / Credit Service Revenue 250. Each balances.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: skipping adjustments and reporting cash-basis numbers. Mistake: adjusting Cash — adjusting entries almost never touch Cash. Exit: (a) Which step follows the adjusted trial balance? (b) Depreciation credits which account? Answers: prepare the financial statements; Accumulated Depreciation.

lessons.title: Analyzing financial statements with ratios
lessons.grammar_note: A ratio is one statement number divided by another — always name both.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compute and interpret four core ratios from a set of statements. Warm-up: which ratio tells you whether short-term bills can be paid?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Statements become useful when you compare their numbers. Four workhorse ratios: current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities) for liquidity; debt-to-equity (total liabilities ÷ total equity) for leverage; net profit margin (net income ÷ revenue) for profitability; and return on assets (net income ÷ total assets) for efficiency. Worked example — Delta Retail has current assets $60,000 and current liabilities $30,000, so the current ratio = 60,000 ÷ 30,000 = 2.0, meaning $2 of current assets back every $1 of current debt.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Delta Retail's full set: total liabilities $80,000, total equity $100,000 (so total assets $180,000, and $80,000 + $100,000 = $180,000 balances), revenue $150,000, net income $15,000. Debt-to-equity = 80,000 ÷ 100,000 = 0.8. Net profit margin = 15,000 ÷ 150,000 = 0.10 = 10%. Return on assets = 15,000 ÷ 180,000 = 0.083 = 8.3%. Each ratio comes straight from figures that already tie to the balanced statements.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Using Delta's numbers, compute: (1) the current ratio; (2) debt-to-equity; (3) net profit margin; (4) return on assets. Answers: (1) 60,000 ÷ 30,000 = 2.0; (2) 80,000 ÷ 100,000 = 0.8; (3) 15,000 ÷ 150,000 = 10%; (4) 15,000 ÷ 180,000 = 8.3%.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading a current ratio of 2.0 as 'twice the profit' — it is liquidity, not earnings. Mistake: mixing total and current figures in one ratio. Exit: (a) Which ratio uses net income and revenue? (b) A current ratio above 1.0 suggests what? Answers: net profit margin; current assets exceed current liabilities.

items.translation: a resource the business owns or controls that has value
items.example: Cash, supplies, and equipment are assets on the balance sheet.

items.translation: an amount the business owes to others
items.example: A bank loan is a liability until it is repaid.

items.translation: the owner's residual claim: assets minus liabilities
items.example: After investing $10,000, the owner's equity was $10,000.

items.translation: an entry on the left side of an account
items.example: Increasing Cash is recorded as a debit.

items.translation: an entry on the right side of an account
items.example: Service Revenue increases with a credit.

items.translation: recording revenue when earned and expense when incurred, not when cash moves
items.example: Accrual accounting recognized the $500 fee even before the client paid.

questions.prompt: The correct order of the accounting cycle ends with…
questions.explanation: Statements are prepared, then the temporary accounts are closed.

questions.prompt: Recording $250 of supplies used requires…
questions.explanation: Expense up with a debit; the Supplies asset down with a credit.

questions.prompt: Adjusting entries almost never affect which account?
questions.explanation: Adjustments correct timing; the cash usually already moved or hasn't yet.

questions.prompt: Current assets $60,000 and current liabilities $30,000 give a current ratio of…
Net income $15,000 on revenue $150,000 is a net profit margin of…
Under accrual accounting, a $500 service performed but not yet billed is recorded as…
options: Debit Accounts Receivable, Credit Service Revenue
questions.explanation: Revenue is earned now; the receivable captures the amount owed.

lessons.title: Applied project: build a set of statements

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Invent a small service business and record one month of activity, then produce its income statement, statement of owner's equity, and balance sheet. You will not use software — you will show that your books balance by hand.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) List 6–8 transactions (an investment, a purchase, at least one on account, some revenue, some expenses, one owner withdrawal). 2) Journalize each so debits equal credits. 3) Compute net income = Revenue − Expenses. 4) Roll net income into ending equity. 5) Prepare a balance sheet and confirm Assets = Liabilities + Equity.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Every journal entry has equal debits and credits. ✔ Net income is Revenue minus Expenses only (no withdrawals). ✔ Ending equity = investment + net income − drawings. ✔ The balance sheet balances: total assets equal total liabilities plus equity. If all four hold, your statements are internally consistent — you've closed the loop like an accountant.
